stages.name: Regulating monopoly
stages.title: Regulating monopoly
stages.sub: How regulators cap prices, cap profits and set quality standards, and what each tool costs.

steps.q: A water monopoly is exploiting customers with high prices. A regulator tells it it may only raise its average price by inflation minus 2% each year. What has the regulator directly limited?
steps.right: How much the firm can charge
steps.wrong: How much profit the firm can keep
steps.hint: The rule is written in terms of what customers pay, not what the firm earns.

steps.q: Instead of capping charges, the regulator now tells the same firm it cannot earn more than an 8% return on the capital it has invested. What has the regulator limited this time?
steps.right: How much the firm can keep as profit
steps.wrong: How much the firm can charge customers
steps.hint: The rule is written in terms of return earned, not the price on the bill.

steps.q: Before the cap, the monopoly was earning huge profits by charging high prices with little competition to stop it. After the 8% cap, can it keep piling on the same excess profit?
steps.right: No, its profit is now held down
steps.wrong: Yes, the cap does not change this
steps.hint: Think about what the cap was designed to stop the firm doing to consumers.

steps.q: Under the 8% rule, if the firm cuts its costs, its allowed profit stays tied to capital employed rather than to how efficiently it runs. Does the firm now gain much extra reward for cutting costs?
steps.right: Not really, the reward for cutting costs is weak
steps.wrong: Yes, cutting costs still boosts its reward a lot

steps.q: A regulator now requires the water firm to answer 95% of complaints within 48 hours and fix leaks within a set number of days, checking and fining it if it fails. What kind of rule is this?
steps.right: A minimum level of service the firm must meet
steps.wrong: A limit on the price the firm can charge
steps.hint: The rule is about speed and reliability of service, not about money charged or earned.

steps.right: No, it adds costs that can be passed on
steps.wrong: Yes, monitoring and compliance cost nothing
